claim: CUDA++ is the GPU half of Omega, plus the motor.
claim_rest: It runs on the NVIDIA GPUs people already own, with no NVIDIA user-space software: no CUDA toolkit, no nvcc, no PTX, no libcuda, no cuBLAS. It is its own open source project, under the Apache License 2.0 with the LLVM exception, in the repository aien-dev/CUDApp.
It runs on the NVIDIA GB10 in the DGX Spark today. On 2026-10-21 the 35 billion parameter model Aien serves on the Spark was running on this code with zero CUDA libraries loaded.
purpose_title: Less computation, out of the big data centers.
purpose: The goal is not a faster way to rent a data center. It is to need less of one: the same work with fewer bytes moved, fewer operations and fewer joules per answer, so it runs on a machine a person owns (a DGX Spark, a PC with one graphics card, a laptop). Every result is reported as work per answer, against the machine's own ceiling.
private_note: The repository is public: https://github.com/aien-dev/CUDApp. Its audit is https://github.com/aien-dev/CUDApp/blob/main/docs/AUDIT.md (Status CLEAN).

hops.ours: Aien's own GB10 driver. Its simulator gates pass; it has not run on the chip yet.
Stays NVIDIA's. The chip checks the firmware's signature and boots nothing else. CUDA++ never ships it.

how_lead: I build this with AI coding agents, on one DGX Spark, in four weeks. NVIDIA publishes the source of its Linux kernel module, but not its compiler, its driver library or the GPU's machine code. So I skipped every closed layer.

steps.title: 1. The driver client, from the open kernel module's headers
steps.text: libcuda is closed, but everything it does to the hardware goes through ioctls that the open kernel module defines in its public headers. I copied 67 of those headers unchanged (MIT) and wrote my own client against them: client, device, address space, memory, command ring, compute object, doorbell, completion.

steps.title: 2. The machine code, reverse engineered
steps.text: NVIDIA does not publish the GPU's instruction encoding. I compiled small probe kernels of my own once with NVIDIA's compiler, read the machine code back with NVIDIA's disassembler as an offline oracle, and compared kernels that differ in one detail to see which bits mean what. I cross-checked against Mesa's open NVIDIA compiler, NAK, and believed nothing until the chip ran it and gave the right answer. The tensor-core arithmetic was measured on the chip over 2,048 cases until one model matched every output bit.

steps.title: 3. Launches in NVK's order
steps.text: A launch on Blackwell is a short list of commands in the channel ring. I took their order from Mesa's NVK Vulkan driver and the method offsets from the open headers, built my own command lists, and measured them: about 24 to 31 microseconds per extra dependent launch.

steps.title: 4. Built up, nothing counts until the chip agrees
steps.text: 2026-09-26 vector add on the GB10. 2026-10-02 numerics closed on the chip. 2026-10-13 my own probes measured the tensor cores at 115.14 TFLOPS and memory reads at 195.1 GB/s. 2026-10-21 a 35B model served on this code with zero CUDA libraries in the process.

did_not: No NVIDIA source code other than the open kernel module headers, and no NVIDIA binary. No libcuda, cubin, PTX or firmware in the repository or its history.
I did not take apart libcuda, nvcc or any other NVIDIA program. I ran NVIDIA's compiler and disassembler on my own small kernels and read what they printed.
I did not touch the GPU's firmware. It is still NVIDIA's, and the chip checks its signature.
I did not translate CUDA programs to run on other hardware. CUDA++ runs on NVIDIA GPUs, the ones people already paid for.
pain_lead: What makes CUDA hard to use and hard to leave, how CUDA++ fixes each one, and the command that shows it. A row is marked fixed only with its receipt.

pains.title: CUDA's pain points and the fix for each
pains.text: Being written in docs/PAIN_POINTS.md and a README section of CUDA++: each pain point people report, how CUDA++ answers it, and the one command that shows the answer.

swap_lead: Take CUDA off a machine and put CUDA++ in its place, all the way down to the kernel driver, with one command each way.

swaps.title: User space: cudapp swap
swaps.text: A drop-in libcuda.so.1 on the CUDA++ runtime, so a CUDA program runs unmodified on CUDA++. One command in, one command back. Written up in docs/SWAP.md.

swaps.title: Kernel driver: cudapp swap kernel
swaps.text: Packaging, switch and rollback that replace nvidia.ko and nvidia-uvm.ko with Aien's own GB10 driver. L401 builds the packaging; L332 builds the driver, whose simulator gates pass and which has not run on the chip yet.
